title: Yosef Karo and the Shulchan Aruch

trailer.text: According to the New World Encyclopedia, Rabbi Yosef Karo was one of the most significant writers in rabbinic Judaism, and the author of the Shulchan Aruch.
He was born to a Spanish Jewish family, and he and his parents were forced to move first to Portugal and then to what is today Bulgaria.
He began writing his great work, the Bet Yosef, at Adrianople and finished it at Safed.
He then wrote an abridged version of it, the Shulchan Arukh, in a manner accessible also to those who were not scholars.
According to EBSCO, the Shulchan Aruch, together with Rabbi Moses Isserles's commentary on Ashkenazi customs, became the basis of Jewish law into the 21st century.

stations.title: A child on the roads of expulsion

paragraphs.text: According to the New World Encyclopedia, Yosef Karo was born to a Spanish Jewish family.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he was born in Spain or Portugal in 1488.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, he was expelled with his family in the expulsion from Spain.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, he and his parents were forced to move first to Portugal and then to what is today Bulgaria.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he received his first instruction from his father.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, his father died in his childhood, and he grew up in the home of his uncle, Rabbi Yitzhak Karo.

stations.title: Scattered law in a changed world

paragraphs.text: According to EBSCO, before Karo, Jewish law was a collection of decisions and interpretations of rabbis through the ages.
According to EBSCO, the work of Maimonides represented mainly Sephardic laws and customs, and it generally lacked Talmudic references.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the expulsion from the Pyrenean peninsula and the invention of printing endangered the stability of the observance of law and custom.
According to the same source, the exiles came to communities in the East and West, where usages entirely different from those they had known prevailed.
Printed books spread halakic literature, and according to the Jewish Encyclopedia many half-educated persons felt justified in following any ancient authority at will.
According to EBSCO, the array of sources and commentaries frustrated rabbinic scholars.
According to EBSCO, Karo hoped to write a definitive description of the law.

stations.title: The Bet Yosef: the great book

paragraphs.text: According to EBSCO, Karo lived in Turkey approximately forty years, and there he began his most important work.
According to EBSCO, in his wanderings among the cities of Turkey he was influenced by Kabbalists such as Solomon Alkabetz and Joseph Taitazak.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, between 1520 and 1522 he settled at Adrianople, where he probably met Solomon Molcho, who strengthened his mystical tendencies.
In 1522 he began writing the Bet Yosef.
According to EBSCO, in the book he kept the chapter divisions of the Tur.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the book briefly sums up and critically discusses thirty-two authorities, from the Talmud to the works of Isserlein.

According to the same source, Karo took Alfasi, Maimonides and Asher b. Jehiel as his standards and accepted the opinion of two of the three, except in cases where most of the early authorities disagreed with them; in practice, however, he more than once decided independently according to his own opinion.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, no other rabbinical work can compare with the Bet Yosef in wealth of material.
He finished the book at Safed in 1542, and published it in the years 1550 to 1559.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, after several years at Salonica and Constantinople, Karo arrived in the Land of Israel.
According to EBSCO, he left Turkey and eventually made his way to Safed.
According to EBSCO, Safed was then a center of Jewish life in the Ottoman Empire and a gathering point for the study of Kabbalah.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, at Safed Karo met Jacob Berab, who exerted a great influence upon him.
According to EBSCO, Karo was one of the few scholars ordained by Berav.
According to EBSCO, when Berav left Safed in 1538, Karo was acknowledged as the leading scholar in the city.
According to EBSCO, he headed the yeshivah in Safed and became the leading authority on questions of Halakhah.
According to the Posen Library, he was a central member of the kabbalist circles in Safed.

According to EBSCO, during the period when he wandered among the cities of Turkey, before he moved to Safed, Karo studied together with Alkabetz, and during their joint study he developed the custom of studying all night on the holiday of Shavuot.

stations.title: The Shulchan Aruch: the abridged book

paragraphs.text: According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, the Shulchan Aruch was written as a summary of Karo's book on the Tur.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, Karo wrote it in his old age, for the benefit of those who did not have the knowledge to understand the longer and more complex Bet Yosef.
According to EBSCO, it is an abridged version of the Beit Yosef, written in a manner accessible also to those who were not scholars.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, the book comprises four parts: Orach Chayim, Yoreh De'ah, Even HaEzer and Choshen Mishpat.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, in it Karo generally rules according to the three pillars of instruction.
According to EBSCO, his works presented the law in a format accessible to both scholars and laypersons.

According to an English translation of the introduction to the Shulchan Arukh, Karo presents himself in it as an insignificant man, Joseph Karo, son of the great R. Ephraim, son of the great R. Joseph Karo.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, Karo himself did not hold a very high opinion of the book, and said that he had written it chiefly for young students.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the Shulchan Aruch was printed in Venice in 1565.
According to EBSCO, the Shulchan Aruch primarily reflected Sephardic customs.
According to EBSCO, in 1569 Rabbi Moses Isserles of Poland wrote a commentary dealing with Ashkenazi customs, to address this gap.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Karo held fast to the original authorities and material reasons, while Isserles considered the minhag a matter of great importance.
According to EBSCO, the Shulchan Aruch together with Isserles's Mappah became the basis for Jewish law into the 21st century.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, at the end of the 16th century the Shulchan Aruch faced competition from the Lebushim of Mordecai Yoffe.
According to the same source, the battle around the book lasted about a hundred years, and by the middle of the 17th century its authority was already firmly established.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, the controversy in fact made the book more popular.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, the Shulchan Aruch was in time accepted as the foundational book of halakhic ruling in most Jewish communities.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, some say that the Sephardim accepted upon themselves the rulings of Maran, whether lenient or stringent.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, dozens of commentaries were written on it, among them Magen Avraham, Turei Zahav, Siftei Kohen and Mishnah Berurah.

According to Wikiyeshiva, the Mishnah Berurah, written on the Orach Chaim section, is considered by many to be the principal halakhic authority of Ashkenazi Jews today in the areas it covers, but this is not agreed upon.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, in the 19th century the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch of Solomon Ganzfried, written for laypersons, became popular in several languages.
According to the same source, the Shulchan Aruch HaRav of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi serves many Hasidim as the basis for daily life.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, the Shulchan Aruch is the nearly universally accepted guide in Orthodox Judaism.
According to the Yeshiva.org.il wiki, Karo was the chief of the rabbis of Safed, a halakhic decisor and a Kabbalist.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in the last thirty years of his life his reputation was greater than that of almost any other rabbi since Maimonides.
According to the same source, members of the community of Carpentras, in France, who felt unjustly treated in a matter of taxes, also appealed to him.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, he was also a key leader of the Jewish community of the Land of Israel in his time.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, he ordained his pupil Moses Alshech.
According to the same source, the opposition to establishing a new authority for rabbinical ordination was too great, and in the end he gave up the endeavor.
According to EBSCO, his commentary Kesef Mishneh remains the standard commentary on eight of the fourteen volumes of the Mishneh Torah.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the book Maggid Mesharim is a kind of diary in which Karo, over a period of fifty years, noted his discussions with the Maggid, the personified Mishnah.
According to a Kabbalistic tradition cited by EBSCO, the Maggid first visited him during one of the night sessions.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the diary stresses asceticism, and in it Karo is often severely rebuked for taking more than one glass of wine or for eating meat.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, the authorship of the diary is disputed, and the view of Karo as a mystic is based in part on the assumption that it is authentic.
According to EBSCO, Karo was married four or five times, and fathered at least one son while in his eighties.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he died at Safed on March 24, 1575.
According to the same source, his death caused general mourning, and funeral orations delivered at the time have been preserved.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, critics denigrated the Shulchan Aruch as overly simple.
According to the same source, Solomon Luria argued that only the more ancient commentators are authoritative.
According to the New World Encyclopedia, the opposition to the work is sometimes seen as a protest of Ashkenazi Jews against the intellectual supremacy of the Sephardim.
According to the same source, Karo's authority was so great that even his opponents accepted it with humility.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, adversaries of the Jews used passages from the Shulchan Aruch, detached from their context and sometimes distorted, to represent the religion of the Jews as dangerous and despicable.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, קארו החזיק במקורות קדומים ובנימוקים עניינים, ואילו איסרליש ראה במנהג דבר חשוב מאוד.

claims.text: לפי New World Encyclopedia, המאבק סביב השולחן ערוך נמשך כמאה שנה, ובאמצע המאה ה-17 סמכותו הייתה מבוססת היטב.

claims.text: לפי ויקישיבה, קארו חיבר את השולחן ערוך, ספר ההלכה הבסיסי שנתקבל ברוב תפוצות ישראל כספר היסוד בפסיקת הלכה.

claims.text: לפי ויקישיבה, השולחן ערוך התקבל עם הזמן כספר ההלכה היסודי ברוב קהילות ישראל.

claims.text: לפי ויקישיבה, נכתבו עשרות פירושים לשולחן ערוך, ובהם מגן אברהם, טורי זהב, שפתי כהן ומשנה ברורה.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, מגיד מישרים מדגיש סגפנות, וקארו נוזף שם פעמים רבות על שתיית יותר מכוס יין אחת או על אכילת בשר.
